correctness.rationale: The 14-facet body has 24 vertices and 36 nearest-neighbor edges, each with endpoint cosine 4/5. Every generic normal reduces by signed permutations to exactly five feasible sign chambers, and exhaustive integer edge-crossing counts show section sizes 6, 8 or 10 as tabulated. The ten-sided chamber is a spherical triangle with exact determinant 1 and denominator 11+3sqrt(14)+4sqrt(6)+2sqrt(21). Its solid angle gives p10; the independent edge-angle expectation and normalization give p6 and p8. A reproducible standalone checker independently reconstructs 605 sections from facet equations. The finite tests corroborate, rather than replace, the continuum proof. Boundary normals have zero spherical measure.

originality.rationale: Actual similarity retrieval for the BCC Voronoi cell, Kelvin-cell/truncated-octahedron slicing and its 6/8/10 angular law returned no direct statement. The same-body closest inspected full manuscript (Cesaroni-Novaga 2026) establishes isoperimetry, not Haar section statistics. The earlier full text (De Loera et al. 2024) treats attainable vertex counts but not this angle-integrated distribution. Known exact laws for other solids, and the prior same-body shadow-area result, do not mathematically imply the present law without the new chamber classification. One related 2026 slicing manuscript remained full-text inaccessible, and historical alias priority remains a documented risk.

value.rationale: The BCC Voronoi (regular truncated-octahedral) cell is a canonical space-filling three-dimensional convex body singled out by recent isoperimetric research. Its random central polygon complexity is a natural stereological invariant; determining all possible side counts AND their exact Haar probabilities closes this explicit model, with a nontrivial decagonal spherical cone and an independent 36-edge expected-count identity. The result is not a one-off arbitrary parameter choice or mere recomputation of a known table; the 24-vertex five-chamber structure is distinct from previously evaluated Platonic bodies. This is finite-dimensional and specialized, not a claim of a general new slicing theorem.
